analysis.one_liner: Requires OSHA to issue mandatory rules protecting workers from explosive combustible dust in factories.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or hearing; it sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Labor to issue an interim workplace safety standard—effective 30 days after issuance—requiring factories that handle materials like sugar, wood, plastics, and metal dust to assess explosion hazards, control dust buildup, install ventilation and dust-collection controls, and train and involve workers, based on existing National Fire Protection Association standards. It responded to a documented series of deadly dust explosions and was written to take effect years faster than OSHA's own slow rulemaking process. It was referred to committee and never received a markup or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at the many types of facilities the bill covers—sugar and food plants, wood and furniture shops, plastics, pharmaceutical, textile, and metal facilities—where accumulated dust can ignite and kill. The bill's own findings cite 281 dust incidents between 1980 and 2005 that killed 119 workers and injured 718, and 24 more explosions or fires in the three years after the 2008 Imperial Sugar disaster that killed 4 and injured 65.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a hazard assessment and a written safety program covering dust inspection, ignition control, housekeeping, and safe dust removal, with engineering controls such as ventilation that captures fugitive dust and enclosure of dust-generating processes.
Requires employee and union participation in hazard assessment, incident investigation, and compliance, plus annual safety training for managers and workers.

Sets the interim standard to take effect 30 days after issuance, with a phase-in allowed for engineering controls, bypassing the years-long normal OSHA rulemaking process that the bill says would leave workers exposed for at least four more years.

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that manufacture or handle combustible dusts—food and sugar processors, wood products and furniture makers, plastics, pharmaceutical, textile, and metal fabricators—would bear the cost of hazard assessments, housekeeping programs, ventilation and dust-collection equipment, and training. Many employers already follow the voluntary NFPA standards the bill would make mandatory, so the sharpest costs would fall on those that do not.

drawbacks.text: The bill waives the normal OSHA rulemaking requirements for the interim standard, so it would take effect 30 days after issuance without the usual notice-and-comment process, giving covered facilities little time to prepare and likely inviting legal challenges.

Compliance costs—ventilation systems, dust collection, enclosure of processes, and written programs—would be substantial for some facilities, and small manufacturers would face the same requirements as large ones, though the bill allows a phase-in period for engineering controls.

The bill bases the standard on National Fire Protection Association codes written primarily as fire-prevention standards, which may not map perfectly onto workplace regulation and would need OSHA adaptation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public stakes are life and limb: the record documents 119 deaths and 718 injuries from dust explosions over 25 years, including 14 workers killed in a single 2008 refinery explosion, and the bill adopts controls that many employers already use voluntarily and that a 1987 grain-dust standard proved effective. The offsetting costs are real compliance spending by industry, concentrated on firms that had not adopted the voluntary standards. The main design weakness is speed: forcing an interim standard effective in 30 days without normal rulemaking traded deliberateness for urgency, which is a defensible trade given the documented death toll but a legitimate ground for objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 8, 2011, by Rep. George Miller and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on March 4, 2011, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 112th Congress.
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without a committee vote, a floor vote, or action in the Senate.

The bill's findings documented the hazard it targeted: 281 combustible dust incidents between 1980 and 2005 killing 119 workers and injuring 718, and 24 additional explosions or fires in the three years after the 2008 Imperial Sugar explosion, with 4 deaths and 65 injuries.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of facilities handling combustible dust avoided the mandate to install ventilation, dust-collection, and housekeeping controls, while workers in those plants remained covered only by no comprehensive OSHA dust standard and a rulemaking the bill said would take at least four more years.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: Ranking Member, House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited its only cosponsors.

for.name: U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board
for.what_they_did: Investigated deadly dust explosions and repeatedly recommended that OSHA issue a comprehensive combustible dust standard; the bill's findings cite its reports.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or hearing.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and the bill drew no Republican cosponsors; with Republicans holding the House majority and chairing the committee of referral, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: A quarter of recorded dust explosions occurred at food industry facilities, including the 2008 Imperial Sugar refinery blast that killed 14 workers. The bill would require housekeeping programs, ventilation, and dust-control equipment at these plants.
Wood dust is explicitly covered, so sawmills, cabinet shops, and furniture plants would face mandatory hazard assessments, ignition control, and dust-removal requirements.
Plastics, pesticides, and pharmaceutical dusts are covered; firms would bear engineering-control and training costs, many for hazards they already manage voluntarily under NFPA standards.
